subject: English
topic: Error Detection — Advanced Grammar for SSC CGL Tier 2 (W10 B2)

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) Neither the employees / (B) nor the manager / (C) were willing to accept responsibility / (D) No error
questions.explanation: C is correct. With 'Neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. Here the nearer subject is 'the manager' (singular), so the verb should be 'was willing', not 'were willing'. Rule: Neither A nor B + verb agrees with B. Trap: students applying plural agreement throughout when they see 'employees' first.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) The news about / (B) the devastating floods / (C) were very disturbing / (D) No error
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'News' is an uncountable noun that always takes a singular verb. The correct form is 'was very disturbing.' Other uncountable nouns that fool students: furniture, information, advice, luggage, equipment — all singular. Trap: 'floods' (plural) in part B misleads students into using 'were'.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) He said / (B) that he is / (C) feeling unwell and would leave early / (D) No error
questions.explanation: B is correct. In reported (indirect) speech, when the reporting verb is in the past tense ('said'), the reported clause also shifts to the past: 'is' becomes 'was'. Correct: 'He said that he was feeling unwell.' Note: Part C correctly uses 'would' (past of 'will') already applying backshift. Part B fails to apply it.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) I prefer / (B) coffee / (C) than tea / (D) No error
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Prefer' takes 'to' not 'than'. Correct: 'I prefer coffee to tea.' This is a fixed collocation: prefer X to Y. Trap: students confuse it with the comparative construction 'I like coffee more than tea' (which uses 'than'). SSC Tier 2 tests this distinction regularly.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) Five years have passed / (B) since he has left / (C) the company and moved abroad / (D) No error
questions.explanation: B is correct. After 'since' used to indicate a point in the past, the verb in the subordinate clause should be in the simple past, not the present perfect. Correct: 'since he left'. Rule: since + simple past (point in time); for + present perfect (duration). Trap: 'have passed' in Part A uses the present perfect correctly for the main clause duration.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) The furniture in the hall / (B) were of excellent quality / (C) and had been imported / (D) No error
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun treated as singular. The verb should be 'was of excellent quality.' Like 'news', 'furniture' cannot be made plural and always takes singular verb agreement. Trap: 'hall' is close to the verb and is singular (irrelevant); the head noun 'furniture' controls agreement.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) No sooner did / (B) he arrive at the station / (C) when the train departed / (D) No error
questions.explanation: C is correct. The correlative construction 'No sooner...than' is a fixed pair — 'when' cannot replace 'than'. Correct: 'No sooner did he arrive at the station than the train departed.' SSC regularly tests these correlative conjunctions: No sooner...than, Hardly/Scarcely...when, As soon as...than (wrong — 'as soon as' stands alone). Trap: 'when' feels natural after the pause implied by 'arrive at the station.'

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) He is / (B) more cleverer / (C) than his sister / (D) No error
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'More cleverer' is a double comparative — an error. Either 'cleverer' (inflected form) OR 'more clever' is correct, but not both together. Similarly forbidden: 'more better', 'most kindest', 'more happier'. Trap: students sometimes accept double comparatives in informal speech, but they are grammatical errors in standard English tested by SSC.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) The number of students / (B) attending the lecture / (C) were very large / (D) No error
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'The number of' is singular — it refers to the number itself, not the items counted. Correct: 'was very large'. Compare with 'A number of students WERE attending' (A number of = many, takes plural). This 'the number of' vs. 'a number of' distinction is a favourite SSC Tier 2 error spotting trap.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with a grammatical error:
(A) Each of the fifteen contestants / (B) who participated in the final round / (C) were awarded a certificate / (D) No error
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Each' is always singular, regardless of the plural noun that follows it in 'each of the + plural noun'. The verb must be 'was awarded', not 'were awarded'. Rule: Each, Every, Either, Neither, One of — all take singular verbs. The long relative clause 'who participated in the final round' distracts students from the head subject 'Each'.
